sentences.text: The genus Sarcosuchus includes the type species Sarcosuchus imperator, a massive predator where the largest known skull measures 1.6 meters in length, leading to an estimated total body length of 11.65 meters.
This animal featured telescoped eyes and a snout that accounted for 75% of the skull's length, while possessing 35 teeth on each side of the upper jaw and 31 teeth on each side of the lower jaw.

Fully grown individuals are estimated to have reached lengths of 9 to 9.5 meters and weights of 3.45 to 4.3 metric tons, though O'Brien et al. (2019) estimated the largest specimen was nearly 9 meters long and weighed 3.45 metric tons.

Fossils were first discovered in the 1850s in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, by Samuel Allport, but the genus was not formally described until 1966 by Frances de Broin and Philippe Taquet based on an incomplete skull found in Gadoufaoua, northern Niger.

In 1964, a French Atomic Energy Commission team discovered a nearly complete crocodylomorph skull at Gadoufaoua while searching for uranium, and in 1977, the species formerly known as Crocodylus hartti was reassigned to the genus Sarcosuchus.

Sarcosuchus is considered a generalist predator, unlike most other pholidosaurids which were specialized fish eaters, and isotopic analyses suggest it had a diet consisting of both fish and large dinosaurs.

Biomechanical analyses indicate that Sarcosuchus was not capable of performing a crocodile-like 'death roll', leading to debate over whether it had a lifestyle similar to the Nile crocodile, hunting large terrestrial prey.

Sarcosuchus is classified within the clade Pholidosauridae, which is related to but distinct from the group containing modern crocodiles and alligators, and is most closely related to the North American genus Terminonaris.
Sarcosuchus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically the Hauterivian to Albian ages, in North Africa and Brazil, where the Gadoufaoua locality dates to between 125 and 112 million years ago.

During this time, these regions were covered in mangrove forests and wetlands, creating a biodiversity hotspot where Sarcosuchus coexisted with theropod dinosaurs and other crocodiles, living near river banks.
Some researchers argue that estimates of S. imperator size based on modern crocodilian correlations are significantly larger than reality.
